hook: Collide two gliders on an air track and watch total momentum stay put while kinetic energy goes missing, then crash a glider into a force sensor and design a crumple zone that keeps the peak force low.
outcome: Show with momentum and energy ledgers that total momentum is conserved in every collision while kinetic energy depends on the bounciness e, and use impulse as the area under a force-time graph to design a nose that lowers the peak force
sources: OpenStax, University Physics Volume 1, chapter 9, sections 9.3 to 9.6: conservation of momentum, elastic and inelastic collisions, center of mass (CC BY 4.0): https://openstax.org/books/university-physics-volume-1/pages/9-introduction
OpenStax, College Physics 2e, section 8.2 Impulse: impulse equals change in momentum, longer contact time lowers force (CC BY 4.0): https://openstax.org/books/college-physics-2e/pages/8-2-impulse
HyperPhysics, Coefficient of Restitution, and OpenStax University Physics Volume 1, section 9.4: http://hyperphysics.phy-astr.gsu.edu/hbase/elacol.html

OpenStax, University Physics Volume 1, sections 7.1, 7.2 and 15.1: work by a constant force, spring force and energy, period of a mass on a spring: https://openstax.org/books/university-physics-volume-1/pages/15-1-simple-harmonic-motion
Every preset and reference result recomputed in Python (closed forms and an independent velocity Verlet run) and checked against the tool's own engine (2026-10-25)
Glider masses, spring constants, crush forces and the four design specs are invented lab settings, not real equipment ratings or crash standards
Track, gliders, noses, sensor wall, bars, graphs and plots drawn in code; sounds generated in the browser
Narration generated with Qwen3-TTS (Apache 2.0), cloning a Google Gemini text-to-speech voice
